title: Tristan und Isolde
facts: Tristan und Isolde premiered in Munich on 10 June 1865, conducted by Hans von Bülow.
The premiere, planned for 15 May 1865, was postponed because the Isolde, Malvina Schnorr von Carolsfeld, was hoarse. Her husband Ludwig sang Tristan.
The opera was inspired partly by Schopenhauer’s philosophy and by Wagner’s relationship with his muse, Mathilde Wesendonck.
Wagner to Liszt, 1854: “Never in my life having enjoyed the true happiness of love I shall erect a memorial to this loveliest of all dreams.”
Wagner, letter to Franz Liszt (via Wikipedia)
The “Tristan chord” in the Prelude marks a defining moment in music history: chromaticism, tonal ambiguity and prolonged harmonic suspension.
The harmonic tension set up in the Prelude isn’t fully resolved until the very end of Act III.
Critic Eduard Hanslick, 1868: the Prelude reminded him of an old painting of a martyr whose intestines are slowly unwound on a reel.
Emmanuel Chabrier reportedly wept at the opening: “I’ve been waiting for ten years of my life for that A on the ’cellos.”
Clara Schumann called Tristan “the most repugnant thing I have ever seen or heard in all my life”.
Verdi said, shortly before his death, that he “stood in wonder and terror” before Tristan.
Richard Strauss first said Wagner’s music “would kill a cat”. Later, after conducting his first Tristan: “It was the most wonderful day of my life.”
Mark Twain at Bayreuth: “I know of some, and have heard of many, who could not sleep after it, but cried the night away.”
At the climax of the love duet, the expected resolution is cut off by Kurwenal’s cry: “Rette Dich, Tristan!”
Ravel parodied this love duet as a duet for two cats in L’enfant et les sortilèges.
Only after Isolde’s “Liebestod” does the music fully resolve; she sinks down, “as if transfigured”, onto Tristan’s body.
Wagner himself called the Prelude the “Liebestod” and Isolde’s final aria the “Verklärung” (Transfiguration).
The first Tristan, Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld, died suddenly in July 1865 after singing the role only four times.
Two conductors, Felix Mottl (1911) and Joseph Keilberth (1968), died after collapsing while conducting Act II of Tristan.
The Met gave the first American performance on 1 December 1886, with Lilli Lehmann and Albert Niemann.
